MARKET.head: Bordeaux holds trading lead as Burgundy's share slips, Lynch-Bages 2005 top-traded
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux led the Liv-ex market with a 37.4% share of purchases, and Lynch-Bages was the top-traded wine overall.
Burgundy's share fell to 15.4% from 18.4% last week, below a September average of 24.6%.
US buyers claimed over half of Bordeaux's purchased value, lifting the US share of trade to 9.6% from 7.0%.

MARKET.head: Surrey funds 17 rural projects, including a vineyard bird-repelling laser
MARKET.summ: A wine producer using bird-repelling lasers and cattle farmer using GPS collars to track livestock are among 17 innovative projects funded from a £500,000 pot to boost Surrey’s rural economy. Surrey County Council’s Farming Innovation Accelerator supports farmers and growers with funding for projects to modernise operations,...
takeaways: Surrey County Council's Farming Innovation Accelerator is funding 17 rural and farming projects from a £500,000 pot.
Each of the 17 recipients receives a grant of up to £35,000 plus expert business support, drawn from UK Shared Prosperity Funding.
Albury Vineyard will install an automated bird-repellent laser to protect 18 acres of vines, adding over 1,700 bottles yearly.

MARKET.head: Navarra's costly Saignée rosé shows how winemakers can turn difficulty into premium value
MARKET.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra's rosado uses the Saignée method, which can need up to three times more grapes than standard red production.
Navarra's new Rosado Tradition designation requires Saignée and exclusive use of Garnacha, reinforcing its premium positioning.

MARKET.head: Australian wine exports fall 7% to $2.25bn as US and China weaken
MARKET.summ:
Australian wine exports declined overall in the year ending September 2026, but the results varied significantly across markets. Strong growth in Southeast Asia and Canada was offset by more challenging conditions in the United States (US). 

This Market Bulletin will analyse the latest export data, released...
takeaways: Australian wine export value fell 7% to $2.25 billion in the 12 months to September 2026, volume down 5% to 590 million litres.
Exports to the US fell 28% in value to $219 million, driven by tariffs and a shrinking American wine market.
Southeast Asia grew 16% to $291 million, with Thailand up 57% to a record $73 million, while Canada rose 12% to $185 million.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads fine wine trade at 39.6% share, Lafite 2005 tops sales
MARKET.summ: Bordeaux led the market, claiming 39.6%, Lafite accounting for over a quarter of its trade
takeaways: Bordeaux took 39.6% of traded value on the Liv-ex fine wine market, with Lafite the region's top-traded wine at over a quarter of its value.
Burgundy fell from 24.8% last week to 18.4%, while Tuscany rose from 5.2% to 8.9%.
Bollinger overtook Dom Perignon and Louis Roeder as top-traded Champagne producer by value, with R.D. 2008 the leading wine.

MARKET.head: VinePair's weekly roundup covers Supreme Court case, Uncle Nearest sale, and product releases
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.
takeaways: The US Supreme Court agreed to review a home distilling case, per this week's roundup.
Uncle Nearest's potential buyers and Fawn Weaver's motion to block the sale were covered.
Southern Glazer's bribery snafu and OpenTable's 2026 restaurant report also featured this week.

CULTURE.head: South African wine estates confront slavery history as evictions and disputes continue
CULTURE.summ:
Slavery was integral to the country’s wine industry. Now a handful of wineries are addressing its legacy and righting the wrongs of the past

At Groot Constantia, the oldest wine farm in South Africa, the 450,000 visitors who pass through its gates annually can admire the picturesque vineyards sloping towards a bay...
takeaways: Groot Constantia, South Africa's oldest wine farm, runs a museum with panels on the about 30 enslaved people who lived there from 1685 to 1834.
Historians say only a handful of South African estates explicitly acknowledge their history of enslavement, in an industry that sold R36.3bn of wine last year.
At least 10 families, mostly former workers, have been evicted from Groot Constantia since July, according to two advocacy groups.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives drink mass-market, sweet wines, critic argues
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Wine columnist Cake Zine essay argues Real Housewives favour mass-market, high-alcohol, sweet wines, mostly Californian cabernet.
Essay ties this taste to Robert Parker's 100-point system and the 'Parkerization' of wines toward sweeter, fruit-forward styles.
Writer notes fine wines like Pomerol and Romanée-Conti are often unknown to the wider public, unlike Veuve Clicquot or Dom Pérignon.

SCIENCE.head: English vines hit by 2026 heatwaves; harvest 10-14 days early
SCIENCE.summ: With harvest complete, or nearing completion on many vineyards, Hutchinsons agronomists Rob Saunders and Will Robinson look at the impact of the record-breaking summer and what we can learn for future seasons. While 2026 could be remembered as a vintage season for some growers, others will look back less fondly, having first...
takeaways: A 2026 UK viticulture assessment examines how repeated heatwaves and drought affected vines this season.
Fifty-four Met Office stations set all-time daily maximum records this summer, peaking at 38.2°C in Gloucestershire in August.
Harvest ran about 10-14 days earlier than normal, but Bacchus struggled as sugar stalled while acidity kept falling.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards face early, hot 2026 harvest after frost and drought
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: The 2026 growing season began with severe frosts, then turned warm and dry, with rapid ripening across English and Welsh vineyards.
Harvest started several weeks early at some sites, while dry weather kept disease pressure low and fruit healthy.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details organic and water-saving practices at Mendoza winery
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR Membership Manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet, a winery at the foot of the Andes in Mendoza, in February.
The estate is trialing biodiversity and garden vineyard corridors, harvesting from outside the rows, and growing vegetables alongside vines.
Domaine Bousquet switched to high-pressure hoses to cut water use and updated tanks and temperature-controlled rooms to reduce energy.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data validated for mapping vineyard water use in Italy
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: Padova researchers tested MODIS satellite data to estimate evapotranspiration from a 25-hectare northeastern Italian vineyard.
Models combining MODIS data with ground weather observations were calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements.
Independent validation against the other two years showed good consistency, suggesting regional-scale vineyard water monitoring is feasible.

SCIENCE.head: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex battles frost and pests after 2023 planting
SCIENCE.summ: Newick Wine Estate in East Sussex is a place of outstanding tranquillity. Newick Village is situated almost equal distance from both Canterbury and Winchester, two important Cathedral cities in the south of England. It is not surprising therefore that the village has an ancient history.
takeaways: Jonathan and Charlotte Sharpe planted 37,000 vines on half of their 16-hectare East Sussex farm at Newick in 2023.
Ten frost events in 2026 caused severe damage, with the final one on 10 May limiting the estate's harvest.
Vineyard manager Charles Negus and apprentice Linus Holter are trialling methods to control spotted wing drosophila (SWD), which hit the 2025 season.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation shape water use and stomatal control in NE Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: A three-year NE Spain study tested Grenache grafted onto 110-R, 41-B and 161-49C rootstocks, irrigated or non-irrigated.
Non-irrigated vines had higher water use efficiency, and 110-R and 41-B outperformed 161-49C.
Stomatal conductance differences from irrigation persisted all season, suggesting hormonal signals matter more than hydraulic ones.

SCIENCE.head: Italian research urges genetic diversity and climate adaptation for future viticulture
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Pisa University researchers say climate change may extend viticulture to higher latitudes and altitudes, requiring more resistant grapevine genotypes.
Local Italian grapevine varieties are being abandoned in global markets, prompting regional safeguard projects to recover them for biodiversity.
The paper reports viticultural trials on Malvasia of Lazio, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon under Cordon Spur of Conegliano training.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance concept and its seasonal dynamics in viticulture explained
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance is the appropriate balance between a vine's vegetative growth and its reproductive growth, meaning fruit production.
Most quantitative measures, such as yield to pruning weight ratio, are indirect and do not capture seasonal growth dynamics.
A dynamic carbohydrate simulation model can show seasonal patterns of growth needs against canopy carbon supply.

SCIENCE.head: Winter vineyard tools that cut pruning labour and frost losses
SCIENCE.summ: As autumn turns to winter a list of jobs looms large in the calendar. The vines need pruning and the soil needs care and attention. To make these jobs less demanding and costly, different tools can be used.
takeaways: Cordless battery secateurs and a tractor-mounted pre-pruner are popular tools for speeding up winter vine pruning.
Mechanical sweepers pull canes into a row so a flail mower can mulch prunings in the same pass.
Frost protection options include candles, wind machines, and the Ventigel, which combines heat and wind.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial tests chemical and manual thinning to cut Vinhos Verdes yields
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 experiment in Vinhos Verdes tested Ethephon, Prohexadione-calcium and manual bunch thinning on Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Manual bunch thinning cut Borraçal yields about 41% and Loureiro yields about 26% against control vines.
Ethephon at berry buckshot size lowered Loureiro yields 35% and raised its sugar content, while Borraçal gained no quality benefit.

NEWSLETTERS.head: With these twelve wines, Juampi Michellini, Matias Riccitelli, Rafael Urreloja and Derek Mossman Knapp illustrate Argentina and Chile’s precocious ability to express the best in any variety
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Twelve wines, selected by their maker, four from Zorzal and four from Riccitelli, Undurraga and The Garage Wines Company, were
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Riccitelli's Patagonia Bastardo (Trousseau) is 100% from a vineyard planted in the 1970s and was whole-bunch fermented and pressed to foudres.
Undurraga's Terroir Hunter Pinot Noir Trama 2022 comes from limestone in San Antonio Valley, about five kilometres from the ocean, and scored 94/100.
Zorzal's Chardonnay Parcelario 2024 from Uco Valley, grown on limestone-influenced soil, is a 'grand cru'-level wine scored 95/100.

NEWSLETTERS.head: S.O.R.B.E.T Wine Tasting: Nov 8, San Francisco
NEWSLETTERS.summ: I don’t know about you, but I love me a good acronym. S.O.R.B.E.T stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: S.O.R.B.E.T is a wine tasting event on November 8 in San Francisco.
The acronym stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Owendee
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The rituals of service for the holidays, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Wine-related search queries slump in July but rise sharply through October, peaking on December 31, according to Maker's Table.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Domaine de Beudon, a family estate at 890 metres in Valais, is reached by a 90-minute hike or a cable car.
Jacky Granges-Faiss bought the estate in 1971; he died in June 2016 after a caterpillar vehicle reversed over him.
Marion Granges-Faiss now leads winemaking, with ferments on the mountain and ageing and bottling at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's winery in Saillon.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Nasty Not Nice
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Why are people drinking less, when wine is better than ever? I have an idea. Wine is too good.
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues wine's decline in drinking is because wine is too good and the trade too nice, and proposes making it less fun.
Atkin suggests wine merchants adopt car-hire tactics: reserve in advance, collect in person, be told the wine is unavailable and sold extra insurance.
Atkin proposes bottling each barrel separately and selling Bordeaux allocations at a Smithfield-style cash sale, including a journalists' barrel at Primeurs.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Seven Chinon lieux-dits have been officially recognized so far: La Croix Boissée (2018), La Pointevinière (2023), Les Puys, Les Picasses, Les Boulaies (2024), and Vindoux and Les Battereaux (2025).
The Chinon Syndicat launched its lieux-dits project in 2014, the first such initiative among Loire Cabernet Franc appellations, avoiding a formal official hierarchy.
To qualify, a lieu-dit must be delineated on the French cadastre and named on the labels of at least two vignerons who jointly request recognition.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the 2024 Port vintage.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Why Michelin Ratings Still Won’t Tell You Who Actually Made Your Burgundy Wine
NEWSLETTERS.summ: This wine guide explains why no critic's score, not even from a renowned guide like Michelin, truly reveals who made your regional wine. Consumer insight is key
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: Since July, some Burgundy bottles have carried Michelin ratings of one to three grapes, assessed on agronomy, technical mastery, identity, balance and consistency.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Telling a mountain to move
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Delving into the details of change in the DO Montsant wine region of Catalunya
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: DO Montsant, in Catalunya's Priorat area, has revised its bylaws to add certification for 'vi brisat' (orange-style) wines.
Montsant's revised bylaws also create a classification for 'minimal intervention' wines, requiring hand-harvesting, organic certification and spontaneous fermentation.
The author says the region's newer minimal-intervention rules, including a maximum sulfur dioxide limit, have not been published, as the DO has not responded to his request for the figure.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni of Santa Fiora is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
A 2024 document unveiled by the Consorzio del Vino Nobile di Montepulciano shows the term 'Vino Nobile' was first used by the Jesuits in 1766.
In 1806 Thomas Jefferson asked Thomas Appleton for 400 bottles annually of Montepulciano wine from ancient Jesuit vineyards after receiving 473 bottles in 1805.
